title: Heritage sites in Andhra Pradesh: stupas, temples and forts
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Andhra Pradesh: Historical Places Guide
meta_description: Heritage sites in Andhra Pradesh, from the Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda stupas to Lepakshi, Gandikota and Chandragiri, with museums and how to visit.
summary: Andhra Pradesh's heritage is strongest in early Buddhism and in temple building. The Krishna valley holds the Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda stupas, the coast has monasteries at Thotlakonda and Sankaram, and the south has Vijayanagara landmarks such as Lepakshi, Chandragiri and Penukonda. The state has no UNESCO World Heritage Site of its own yet.

sections.h2: Why Andhra Pradesh matters for Indian history
paras: For about a thousand years, from around the 3rd century BCE, the lower Krishna and Godavari valleys were among the busiest Buddhist regions of South Asia. Monasteries grew along river routes and the coast, funded by traders, guilds, lay women and royal families, and their donors are named in hundreds of short inscriptions. The region was later ruled by the Eastern Chalukyas, the Kakatiyas, the Reddi kings, the Vijayanagara empire and the Qutb Shahis, and each left buildings you can still read on the ground.

This makes the state a good classroom for two themes at once: how Buddhism spread through patronage and trade, and how temple architecture developed in the Deccan and the south. Our explainer on [Buddhist caves in India](buddhist-caves-in-india.html) sets the wider context, and the [major dynasties of ancient India](major-dynasties-of-ancient-india.html) guide helps place the rulers named below.

sections.h2: Buddhist and archaeological sites in Andhra Pradesh
paras: The Great Stupa at Amaravati, near ancient Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota), was enlarged over several centuries, with its finest limestone reliefs carved around the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Most of the sculpture was removed in the 19th century and is now divided between the ASI museum on site, the Government Museum in Chennai and the British Museum in London. What survives at Amaravati is the base of the drum and the railing line, so a visit works best when paired with the museum.

Nagarjunakonda was the capital of the Ikshvaku kings, around the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. When the Nagarjuna Sagar dam was built, the valley was excavated and many monuments were rebuilt on a hilltop that is now an island, with a museum. It is one of the clearest cases in India of rescue archaeology before a dam.

Smaller sites are just as rewarding. Bhattiprolu yielded reliquary caskets with inscriptions in an early southern variant of Brahmi, which matters for the history of Indian scripts. Guntupalli has rock-cut monastic caves, including a circular chaitya cave. Near Visakhapatnam, Thotlakonda, Bavikonda and Pavurallakonda were hilltop monasteries looking over the sea, and Sankaram, near Anakapalle, has stupas carved out of the living rock. Students who want to read those donor records can start with [a Brahmi workshop](write-like-asoka-s-scribes-a-brahmi-workshop.html).

Temples here span more than a thousand years. The Undavalli caves near Vijayawada are a multi-storey rock-cut complex usually linked to the 5th to 7th centuries, with a large reclining Vishnu. Draksharamam's Bhimeshwara temple belongs to the Eastern Chalukya period, and the Eastern Ganga temples at Mukhalingam in Srikakulam district show the Kalinga style reaching south.

The great pilgrimage centres, Tirumala, Srikalahasti, Srisailam and Ahobilam, are living temples first. Their walls, however, carry long series of inscriptions recording grants by Chola, Vijayanagara and local rulers, which makes them archives as much as shrines. Srisailam's outer wall has carved panels from the Vijayanagara period.

The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi, built in the 16th century under Vijayanagara rule, is the best single stop for art. Its painted ceilings are among the largest surviving Vijayanagara murals, and the complex has an unfinished kalyana mandapa and a large monolithic Nandi nearby. Lepakshi is on India's tentative list for UNESCO, which is not the same as being inscribed. If you want to understand what you are seeing, our [Dravida temple architecture](dravida-temple-architecture.html) session explains plans, towers and halls before a visit.

After the battle of 1565, the Vijayanagara court moved south, first to Penukonda and later to Chandragiri, near Tirupati. Chandragiri's Raja Mahal and Rani Mahal show a palace style that mixes temple masonry with Indo-Islamic arches. Gandikota, set above a gorge of the Penna river in Kadapa district, has a mosque, a granary and the Madhavaraya temple inside one circuit of walls, and changed hands between Vijayanagara commanders and the Qutb Shahi army in the 17th century.
Kondapalli, near Vijayawada, is a hill fort and also the home of a well known tradition of light wooden toys, which is a useful reminder that heritage in Andhra Pradesh is also made by hand today.

sections.h2: What the Andhra inscriptions tell us
paras: The Buddhist sites of Andhra are unusually well documented by their donors. Short Prakrit inscriptions on railing pillars, slabs and caskets record gifts by merchants, artisans, monks, nuns and women of royal households, often naming their home towns. Read together, they show a society in which trade guilds and lay families, not only kings, paid for monuments. At Nagarjunakonda, Ikshvaku queens are named as leading patrons of Buddhist foundations while the kings themselves performed Vedic rites, a useful case for anyone studying how religions shared space.

Later temple walls continue the habit. Telugu and Sanskrit inscriptions at Draksharamam, Srisailam and Tirumala record land grants, lamps, festivals and the names of officials, which lets historians trace who controlled land and labour in each period. Our session on [temple inscriptions and patrons](temple-inscriptions-patrons.html) teaches groups how to read such records on site.

sections.h2: Is there a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Andhra Pradesh?
paras: Not yet. Of India's 45 World Heritage Sites, none lies in Andhra Pradesh. The Ramappa Temple, often searched alongside it, is in Telangana. Lepakshi is on the tentative list. For the full national list see our page on [UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India](unesco-world-heritage-sites-in-india.html).

sections.h2: Planning a heritage trip in Andhra Pradesh for a group
paras: Distances are large, so it helps to choose one cluster. The Krishna valley (Vijayawada, Undavalli, Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda) suits a three to four day archaeology trip. The north coast (Visakhapatnam, Thotlakonda, Sankaram, Salihundam, Mukhalingam) suits a Buddhism and temples trip. The south (Tirupati, Chandragiri, Lepakshi, Penukonda, Gandikota) suits architecture students.

Nagarjunakonda is reached by boat, so check the ASI or state tourism website before you go. We build [a study tour for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html) around any of these clusters, and private families can ask about [private journeys](journeys.html) with an archaeologist.

sites.note: Buddhist monastery and stupas on a hill above the Vamsadhara river.

sites.note: Eastern Ganga temples in Srikakulam district in a Kalinga style.

faq.q: What are the most famous historical places in Andhra Pradesh?
faq.a: The Amaravati stupa, Nagarjunakonda, the Lepakshi Veerabhadra temple, Tirumala, Srisailam, the Undavalli caves, Gandikota and Chandragiri fort are the best known. For Buddhist archaeology, add Guntupalli, Thotlakonda and Sankaram on the coast and in the Godavari region.

faq.q: How many UNESCO sites are there in Andhra Pradesh?
faq.a: None. Andhra Pradesh has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026. The Lepakshi temple is on India's tentative list, and the Ramappa Temple, inscribed in 2021, is in neighbouring Telangana.

faq.q: Where are the Amaravati sculptures now?
faq.a: They are divided between the ASI museum at Amaravati, the Government Museum in Chennai and the British Museum in London. Seeing one collection and the site together gives the clearest picture of how the stupa looked.

faq.q: Can Talaash Heritage arrange a study tour in Andhra Pradesh?
faq.a: Yes, on request. We design custom study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, usually around one cluster such as the Krishna valley Buddhist sites or the Vijayanagara forts in the south, and can add a lecture before the trip.

posts.hook: A whole valley of monuments was moved uphill before a dam flooded it.
posts.caption: At Nagarjunakonda, archaeologists excavated the Ikshvaku capital and rebuilt key monuments on a hilltop that is now an island. It is one of India's early rescue archaeology projects.
The painted ceilings of the Veerabhadra temple are among the largest surviving Vijayanagara murals. Give your eyes a minute to adjust in the main hall, and avoid flash photography.
